text:
# Gaussian Splatting Deformation

Also called: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Time-varying Gaussian Splatting

## Overview
Gaussian Splatting Deformation extends static 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) to dynamic scenes by maintaining a static canonical set of primitives and predicting time-dependent geometric and appearance offsets . It solves the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video by decomposing the 4D representation into a canonical state and a deformation function . It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields](17161-space-time-neural-irradiance-fields.md) and [Dynamic NeRF](21867-dynamic-nerf.md) by using explicit [differentiable rasterization](#18784-differentiable-rasterization.md) of deformed Gaussians rather than [neural volume rendering](#1576-neural-volume-rendering.md), and from [Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF)](21905-neural-scene-flow-fields-nsff.md) by predicting offsets for discrete primitives rather than continuous scene flow fields .

## Shared principles
Methods in this family handle temporal changes by either conditioning a radiance field on time, predicting explicit deformation or scene flow fields, or deforming canonical primitives [S1, unofficial]. For Gaussian Splatting variants, a static set of 3D Gaussians $\mathcal{G}_{canon}$ is defined in a canonical coordinate system, storing base parameters: mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, [rotation](#19376-rotation.md) $\mathbf{q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^4$ (unit quaternion), scale $\mathbf{s}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, opacity $\sigma_i$, and [spherical harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) coefficients $\mathbf{c}_{SH,i}$ . For a given time $t$, a deformation function $D$ predicts offsets $(\delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta\mathbf{q}, \delta\mathbf{s})$ based on the canonical position and time . The time-varying parameters are computed as:
$$ \boldsymbol{\mu}_i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}_i + \delta\boldsymbol{\mu} $$
$$ \mathbf{s}_i(t) = \mathbf{s}_i + \delta\mathbf{s} $$
$$ \mathbf{q}_i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}_i \otimes \delta\mathbf{q}) $$
where $\otimes$ is [quaternion multiplication](#3474-quaternion-operations.md) and normalization prevents drift [G]. The deformation network $D$ typically takes spatial embeddings of canonical positions and temporal embeddings of time $t$ as input . Rendering uses standard differentiable rasterization or volume integration with the updated primitives, camera pose, and time $t$ [G]. Optimization minimizes photometric loss $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{reg}$, updating Gaussian parameters and network weights via [SGD](#15522-sgd-street-view-synthesis-with-gaussian-splatting-and-diffus.md) .

## Subtopics

### [Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting](6145-sparse-controlled-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
[Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting](#6145-sparse-controlled-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) (SC-GS) is a dynamic scene representation method that utilizes a small set of user-provided or learned sparse control points to drive the deformation of dense 3D Gaussians. Unlike methods that predict deformation per-Gaussian, SC-GS propagates edits across time via a learned deformation prior, resulting in a compact and editable representation. It sets itself apart from siblings like [Deformable 3DGS](#6866-deformable-3dgs.md) by decoupling the deformation network's input from individual Gaussian features, instead relying on spatial interpolation from control points. See [Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting](6145-sparse-controlled-3d-gaussian-splatting.md).

### [Deformable 3DGS](6866-deformable-3dgs.md)
Deformable 3DGS extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by modeling time-dependent geometric and appearance parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video by decomposing the 4D representation into a static canonical set of Gaussians and a deformation function that predicts their state at any time $t$. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting](6145-sparse-controlled-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) by using a direct MLP-based deformation network on per-Gaussian features rather than sparse control points. Builds on [Gaussian Splatting Deformation](22469-gaussian-splatting-deformation.md). See [Deformable 3DGS](6866-deformable-3dgs.md).

### Drive-GS
End-to-end driving simulators [S1, unofficial].

### 4D-Driving-GS
A method that drives time-of-day and weather conditioning for closed-loop simulation [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of deforming canonical primitives for dynamic rendering originated in [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) ([NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)) and was adapted to 3D Gaussian Splatting as the latter gained popularity for real-time rendering. Deformable 3DGS and Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting represent the primary approaches to this problem within the Gaussian Splatting ecosystem . These methods are heavily used in autonomous driving simulation, where they enable the integration of dynamic actors into static backgrounds for closed-loop testing [S1, unofficial].
